analysis.one_liner: Requires states to extend Medicaid to more pregnant women and infants, adding home visits to cut infant deaths.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: a single sponsor with no cosponsors introduced it, it sat in a House subcommittee for two years, and the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every state's Medicaid program to cover pregnant women and babies in families earning up to 185% of the federal poverty line, phased in over two years. It would also have stopped states from counting child care and medical costs against a family's income, dropped asset tests for these groups, and let states pay for nurses or others to visit high-risk pregnant women and newborns at home. The goal was fewer babies dying before their first birthday. It died in subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income pregnant women and infants, especially those in families earning between roughly 100% and 185% of the poverty line who today can be turned away in states with lower income limits, plus high-risk mothers and babies who would gain access to prenatal and postpartum home visitation. Medicaid is jointly funded by the federal government and states, so the federal government would pick up its usual matching share of the expanded coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Phases in mandatory Medicaid coverage of pregnant women and infants up to 185% of the federal poverty level, reaching 150% by July 1998 and 185% by July 1999, with states already above those thresholds held to their own higher limits.

Bars states from counting child care costs necessary for a pregnant woman's employment, and medical or remedial care costs, against family income in the eligibility test, using an income methodology no more restrictive than the state's welfare rules.
Prohibits applying an asset (resource) test to pregnant women and infants eligible for Medicaid, removing savings as a barrier to enrollment.
Lets states add Medicaid coverage of prenatal home visitation for high-risk pregnant women and postpartum home visitation for high-risk infants under one year old, prescribed by a physician.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and states share the cost of the expanded Medicaid coverage and home visits through the program's matching structure; state budgets would absorb their share, and the federal share would come from general federal spending.

drawbacks.text: The expansion is an unfunded mandate on states: it forces every state to cover a larger population and pick up its matching share of the cost, which states that had deliberately kept income limits lower would have had to absorb.
The home visitation benefit is optional, so its effect on infant mortality would have depended entirely on each state choosing to adopt it and fund it.

The bill changed eligibility rules (income methodology, asset tests, higher income thresholds) without an independent financing mechanism, so the cost to combined federal and state budgets was real and unquantified in the bill itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is concrete and large for the families reached: health coverage during pregnancy and infancy, fewer barriers like asset tests and child care cost deductions, and home visits for the highest-risk mothers. The cost is higher Medicaid spending shared by Washington and the states. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how states implement the optional home visits, but the core coverage expansion targets a well-documented gap, and the bill's failure to attract a single cosponsor is not explained by any provision in its text.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Commerce Committee and then its health subcommittee, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended with no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Edolphus Towns introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, the first day of the 105th Congress.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce, which held jurisdiction over Medicaid.
On January 27, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and the record shows no further action, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its two-year life.
The 105th Congress ended January 3, 1999, so the bill died automatically when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's death, but the parties that would have borne its cost, state Medicaid programs and the federal treasury, were spared an expansion they never had to vote on. The bill's sponsors gained nothing, and low-income pregnant women and infants gained nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State Medicaid budgets, spared the cost

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand Medicaid coverage for pregnant women and infants and add home visitation services.

against.name: House Commerce Committee / Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never acted on it; the record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no release from subcommittee in two years.

against.name: 434 other House members
against.what_they_did: None of the other members of the House cosponsored the bill during its two-year life.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the only supporter on record was the Democratic sponsor; with zero cosponsors of either party, the bill never developed a visible partisan shape.

industries.industry: State Medicaid programs and state budgets
industries.note: The bill made coverage up to 185% of poverty mandatory rather than optional, requiring states to spend more on pregnant women and infants. States' fiscal interest in narrower eligibility runs against low-income families' interest in coverage.

States adopting the optional benefit would pay for prenatal and postpartum home visitation, creating a new Medicaid-funded service line for these providers. That money would pay for services aimed at reducing infant deaths.
Enrolling more pregnant women and infants in Medicaid means more covered patients and less uncompensated care for hospitals and clinics serving low-income communities.
